item.title: Planets surviving common envelope evolution should be rare, massive, and orbit very close to their host star
item.description: arXiv:2610.27055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The discovery of exoplanets around white dwarfs uniquely informs our understanding of planetary survival through stellar evolution. Common Envelope (CE) evolution is one of the proposed mechanisms that could shape the orbital architecture of these planets around stellar remnants. In this work, we predict the occurrence rate and orbital separation/planet mass distributions for planets that could form around white dwarfs through CE evolution. We simulate populations of giant-planet systems, sampling initial conditions from observed mass and semi-major axis distributions for main sequence stars. We evolve the host star from main sequence to white dwarf to assess which planetary configurations could survive, and we predict the resulting post-CE planet population. Our results suggest that such planets should be rare, massive, and have very close orbital separations. We find that most of the surviving planets have masses of $>10\,M_{\rm{Jup}}$ and orbital separations $<1.4$ times the tidal disruption radius, $a_{{disrupt}}$ ($\lesssim0.006$ AU, also called the Roche limit), which is in contrast to high eccentricity migration, which produces planets with orbital separations $>2a_{disrupt}$. The properties of CE survivors from our simulations contrast with the known closely-orbiting planet WD 1856+534 b, suggesting a different mechanism may be responsible for its formation.
item.dc:creator: Yadira S. Gaibor, Andrew Vanderburg, Juliette C. Becker, Melinda Soares-Furtado, Saul Rappaport, Tansu Daylan

item.title: Small Collisions, Big Impact: The Sensitivity of Atmospheric Temperatures to Collision-Induced Absorption
item.description: arXiv:2610.27067v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Collision-induced absorption (CIA) data are relevant to determining atmospheric temperatures and, in turn, the habitability of a diverse set of planetary atmospheres. However, these data remain sparse across broad wavelength and temperature ranges. Nevertheless, multiple, sometimes disagreeing, sources of experimental and theoretical data can be available for the same CIA pair. In this paper, we assess the impact of these varying sources on atmospheric temperatures and the limitations that the available data coverage can introduce. In order to inform future measurements and calculations, we test additional cases with extrapolated wavelength and temperature ranges. We first introduce a measure of the importance of CIA opacities depending on pressure and temperature by calculating the Rosseland mean with and without each CIA pair's contribution. Secondly, we employ each CIA source in a radiative transfer model of idealised atmospheres which maximise the effect of the CIA pair of interest. Our findings highlight the uncertainties related to the current data. Temperature differences between CIA data sources range from $\sim$10\,K when sources overlap in wavelength and temperature coverage to >100\,K when spectral gaps or temperature limits differ. Spectral windows or narrow temperature coverage can also hinder the model's convergence of the temperature profile. This work aims to provide guidance on the selection of CIA opacity datasets for atmospheric modelling and to identify the wavelength and temperature regimes in which further laboratory measurements and theoretical calculations are most urgently needed. We publish all our findings in detail in the form of an accessible website.
item.dc:creator: David Dahlb\"udding, Tommaso Grassi, Karan Molaverdikhani, Giulia Roccetti, Barbara Ercolano, Paola Caselli

item.title: Beyond static torques: Self-consistent migration and dynamical trapping of low-mass planets in dusty disks
item.description: arXiv:2610.27071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid inward migration of low-mass planets remains a primary theoretical challenge in planet formation. While recent studies show that the solid component of protoplanetary disks can exert strong positive torques to counteract the negative gas torques, traditional static fixed-orbit models fail to capture the fully coupled dynamics of a migrating planet. In this work, we present 2D high-resolution, two-fluid hydrodynamical simulations using a comoving reference frame to track the self-consistent orbital evolution of embedded planets across a comprehensive six-dimensional parameter space. By allowing the planet to dynamically respond to disk-exerted torques, we identify a wide diversity of migration regimes, involving inward/outward migration and oscillatory radial confinement. We also find that massive cores can overcome dust-induced barriers, experiencing dust-mediated runaway outward or inward migration. Conversely, in dust-rich environments continuous gas-dust momentum exchange combined with planet torques dynamically regenerates co-orbital dust asymmetries, creating robust dynamical attractors where super-Earths undergo stable, oscillatory confinement, effectively halting inward drift without requiring pre-existing pressure bumps or disk substructures. This self-induced trapping mechanism could be relevant in the outer disk, beyond the water-ice line in environments with a enhanced local dust-to-gas ratio, where icy pebbles are moderately coupled to the gas. In low-metallicity or highly diffusive disks, planets generally adopt monotonic inward decay, apart from cases with outward migration. Ultimately, the diversity of these self-consistent trajectories demonstrates that static torque approximations are insufficient. Evaluating fully coupled kinematic feedback is essential for accurately predicting planetary survival and the final architecture of planetary systems.
item.dc:creator: Jose L. Gomez, Pablo Benitez-Llambay, Ximena S. Ramos, Octavio M. Guilera

item.title: Ammonia-Hydrogen Phase Equilibria in Planetary Envelopes from First-Principles-Based Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.27136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ammonia and hydrogen are major constituents of planets within and beyond the solar system, yet how they interact in planetary envelopes is poorly known. We perform large-scale two-phase coexistence simulations of the ammonia-hydrogen system from 500 to 4000 K and 0.1 to 100 GPa, driven by machine-learning interatomic potentials trained on density functional theory calculations. From these we map the compositions of coexisting hydrogen-rich and ammonia-rich phases, and the critical curve that separates conditions of complete miscibility from those of phase separation. The critical temperature increases with pressure, from 500 K at 0.1 GPa to 2000 K near 30 GPa, and we find no phase separation at 3000 and 4000 K up to 100 GPa. The slope of the critical curve decreases substantially between 0.3 and 30 GPa, and the curve nearly flattens above about 30 GPa and 2000 K, where molecules begin to give way to atomic species. The coexistence curves are asymmetric with an ammonia-rich critical composition. For the expected envelope compositions, the phase boundary lies close to, and intersects, published thermal profiles of Uranus and Neptune, implying ammonia may be raining out in these planets today. In contrast, in warm sub-Neptunes such as TOI-270 d, ammonia and hydrogen are likely miscible in all proportions. Together with previous studies, our results suggest that silicates, water and ammonia separate from hydrogen in sequence as planets cool, with implications for their compositional, thermal and structural evolution.
item.dc:creator: Akash Gupta, Austin Guo, Jie Deng

item.title: Analytical Chemistry at the Planetary Frontier
item.description: arXiv:2610.27197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Planetary science depends on chemical measurements made under conditions very different from those in a terrestrial laboratory. This review treats the analytical methods of planetary science as one connected chain, from orbital remote sensing through in-situ measurements by landers and rovers and sample collection and curation, to the micro-analysis of returned material on Earth. Orbital methods, including visible and near-infrared reflectance, thermal emission and gamma-ray and neutron spectroscopy, are discussed first. In-situ techniques are then reviewed, including laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), micro-focus X-ray fluorescence (XRF), deep-ultraviolet Raman and fluorescence spectroscopy, evolved gas analysis with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and miniaturized mass spectrometry. Contamination control and curation practices are described, followed by laboratory techniques such as secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS and NanoSIMS), atom probe tomography (APT), thermal ionization mass spectrometry (TIMS), synchrotron micro-XRF and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy. Accuracy, calibration and reference materials are discussed as the link between in-situ and laboratory data, and the role of chemometrics and data fusion is examined. Flight and laboratory instruments are compared in terms of spatial resolution, detection limit, sample consumption and throughput. Active neutron-gamma spectroscopy planned for the Dragonfly mission to Titan is also discussed. This comparison shows that in-situ and laboratory techniques are complementary. In-situ instruments provide context and select samples, while laboratory techniques provide isotopic, molecular and speciation data that cannot yet be obtained in situ.
item.dc:creator: Mavia Anjum

item.title: Size, Albedo, and Taxonomy of Asteroid (1201) Strenua from Stellar Occultation and ATLAS Photometry
item.description: arXiv:2610.27453v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Context. A multi-chord stellar occultation by (1201) Strenua observed on 26 April 2026 is combined with ATLAS $c$- and $o$-band photometry. Aims. We aim to determine the size and geometric albedo of Strenua and reassess its taxonomic classification. Methods. Four positive chords from a 47-station campaign across Indonesia were fitted within a Bayesian forward-modeling framework to derive an ellipse cross-section and equivalent diameter. ATLAS photometry was modeled using the $H, G_1, G_2$ phase-function system to determine band-specific absolute magnitudes, converted to $H_{\mathrm{V}}$, and combined with the occultation diameter to calculate geometric albedo and update taxonomy. Results. The chords yield semi-axes $a' = 27.49^{+3.90}_{-1.65}$~km and $b' = 14.33^{+2.37}_{-2.69}$~km (position angle $95.3^{+4.9}_{-2.7}$ deg), giving an area-equivalent diameter $D_{\mathrm{eq}} = 39.86^{+2.06}_{-1.66}$~km. Photometric modeling gives $H_c = 11.50 \pm 0.05$~mag ($G_{1,c} = 0.81 \pm 0.08$, $G_{2,c} = 0.04 \pm 0.02$) and $H_o = 11.29^{+0.02}_{-0.03}$~mag ($G_{1,o} = 0.94^{+0.03}_{-0.05}$, $G_{2,o} = 0.01 \pm 0.01$), yielding $H_{\mathrm{V}} = 11.46 \pm 0.05$~mag. The resulting geometric albedo $p_{\mathrm{V}} = 0.029 \pm 0.003$ places Strenua among the darkest primitive asteroids, securely reclassifying it as P-class and resolving its legacy X-complex ambiguity.

item.title: Exomoonlight Sonata: On the Fate of Exomoons Around Migrating White Dwarf Planets
item.description: arXiv:2610.27484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The survival of exomoons around close-in white dwarf planets offers a potential constraint on their migration histories and an alternative pathway to post-main-sequence habitability. We investigate whether moons can survive the tidal circularization of planets via high-eccentricity migration, and consider a hierarchical three-body system (white dwarf-planet-moon) after an initial eccentricity excitation of the planetary orbit. Using an analytic equilibrium tidal model, we compare the evolution of the planetary and satellite orbits and examine the conditions required for an evection resonance. We show that the moons of pseudosynchronously rotating planets always migrate inwards since the planetary corotation radius always exceeds the Hill radius, independent of mass and orbital eccentricities. Comparing the migration timescales for the moon and the planet shows that compact moons undergo rapid tidal decay relative to the outer orbit. However, the wider separations favored by slower migration timescales experience pericenter perturbations whose work constitutes a substantial fraction of the moon's orbital energy. Together, our results indicate that moons likely do not survive during a planet's high-eccentricity migration phase in a three-body configuration.
item.dc:creator: Ritvik Sai Narayan, Joseph R. Livesey, Juliette Becker

item.title: When the core ate the atmosphere
item.description: arXiv:2610.27788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The initial volatile element inventories in a planet's atmosphere, mantle, and core are established by delivery and transport during planetary growth. Conversely, the volatile abundances of Earth's planetary reservoirs record its accretion pathway. We model here volatile transport during planet formation for two different delivery scenarios, via pebble and planetesimal accretion, to predict the volatile inventories of proto-Earth at the end of its main accretion phase. We find that the distributions of volatiles between the atmosphere, mantle, and core exhibit strong sensitivity to volatile delivery timing, metal-silicate partition coefficients, atmosphere-magma solubilities, and planet mass. In particular, the early volatile delivery expected in pebble accretion scenarios substantially enhances core sequestration of hydrogen and carbon relative to continuous delivery during incremental planetesimal accretion. With our fiducial partition coefficients, the pebble accretion model produces a 760 bar carbon-dominated atmosphere with 39 bar of hydrogen and water and a few bars of nitrogen, consistent with volatile concentration estimates for bulk silicate Earth including the atmosphere. The corresponding planetesimal accretion model produces a more massive ($\sim$$1350$ bar) atmosphere with similar composition. The core stores $\sim$$70$% of both the H and the C budget in the early-delivery scenario, but $\lesssim$$50$% in the corresponding continuous delivery scenario. Overall our results demonstrate that substantial amounts of volatiles are sequestered into rocky planet cores during planet formation and that the volatile inventory of bulk silicate Earth was likely established already during the magma ocean phase of planet formation.
item.dc:creator: Vera Sparrman, Anders Johansen

item.title: The T-matrix method for modeling the optical properties of grains in exoplanetary atmospheres
item.description: arXiv:2610.28117v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Observations of exoplanetary atmospheres have revealed a rather complex co-existence between the gaseous and condensed phases, ranging from atmospheres apparently covered in clouds to clear ones, across a myriad of intermediate regimes. The interaction between solids and stellar radiation is of fundamental importance when forward or retrieval models are compared to observations. The simplest approach is to assume spherical particles, whose scattering and absorption properties are readily computed with Mie theory. More advanced computational methods, however, can also treat non-spherical condensates. Among these, the transition matrix approach has proven to provide a rigorous and efficient calculation of the extinction by non-spherical particles over a broad range of sizes and refractive indices. We here focus on the absorption and scattering cross sections of forsterite, spinel and silicon monoxide from the near to the far infrared range for particles of different sizes, with shapes ranging from compact ensembles of spheres to porous aggregates. We find that, depending on the size and the configuration chosen, the differences in extinction can be as high as a factor of 2-3, with structured grains being more efficient absorbers in the near infrared for sizes greater than 1 $\mu$m. In a fiducial transmission spectrum we show that in the $\lambda = 1-5\,\mu$m range the amount of spherical material needed to match the contribution of the structured grains can be a factor 2 higher. Such calculations, available for the community through a Zenodo repository, prove to be useful for interpreting recent and future observations of exoplanetary atmospheres.

item.title: Two Validated Planets and 179 Candidates From a TESS Faint Star Transit Search in the ULTRASAT Fields
item.description: arXiv:2610.28518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The TESS mission is designed to survey the entire sky to find planets most amenable to follow-up observations, and transit searches have therefore focused specifically on bright targets. Faint stars ($T_{mag}>13.5$) have not been systematically searched for planets, despite TESS having the sensitivity necessary to do so, therefore representing a promising avenue for increasing TESS's scientific yield. We utilized TESS's sensitivity for faint stars in particular to find more planets for joint optical-UV studies of exoplanet transits. Observing transits in both UV and optical gives insight into exoplanet atmosphere composition and evolution and remains relatively unexplored due to the lack of UV-capable instruments. ULTRASAT is an upcoming UV space telescope that will perform a high cadence survey suitable for observing exoplanet transits. To increase the sample size of planets capable of observations with ULTRASAT, we performed a transit search of faint stars down to $T_{mag}=16$ in the ULTRASAT high cadence survey fields using TESS light curves optimized for faint stars. Our search recovered 262 planet candidates, of which 181 are new to this work. We also statistically validated 2 of those candidates as bona fide planets. Finally, we estimated the ULTRASAT SNR of both new and existing planet candidates, and found that 113 targets will be detectable with ULTRASAT, which would facilitate the largest study of transiting planets in the visible and UV. This work demonstrates the power of TESS to detect exoplanets around faint stars and provides a catalog of well-vetted transiting planet candidates to observe with ULTRASAT.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Lastovka, Thomas Barclay, Robert F. Wilson, Emily A. Gilbert

item.title: TOI-3686: A Hot Jupiter and Sub-Neptune In A 2:1 Mean-Motion Resonance
item.description: arXiv:2610.28533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hot Jupiters are typically thought to be "lonely", but a small and growing subset of them have been found to have nearby planets in the same system. We present the discovery of a new member of this class of systems, TOI-3686. TOI-3686 c is a hot Jupiter with $P_\mathrm{orb} = 5.078$ days detected by NASA's TESS mission that shows peak-to-peak transit timing variations (TTVs) of 40 minutes, amongst the largest ever observed for a hot Jupiter. A subsequent search of the TESS data revealed the transits of a second planet, TOI-3686 b, a sub-Neptune with $P_\mathrm{orb} = 2.54$~days and peak-to-peak TTVs of 10 hours, $\sim 16\%$ of its orbital period. We characterized the system through photodynamical modeling of photometry from TESS and ground-based facilities, as well as radial velocity measurements from the NEID and MAROON-X spectrographs. We find that the two planets in the TOI-3686 system are deep in a 2:1 mean-motion resonance, making this the only hot Jupiter system currently known to be in a truly resonant configuration, which may be related to its $\lesssim1$~Gyr system age. Systems like TOI-3686 likely formed through a dynamically quiescent pathway and were captured into resonance after migration through a disk, and may represent the high-mass end of processes that occur in compact systems of smaller planets.

item.title: A sub-Earth-sized TESS planet candidate in the nearby M-dwarf binary GJ 774, most likely orbiting GJ 774 A (TIC 351339274)
item.description: arXiv:2610.28575v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small planets transiting the nearest M dwarfs are the terrestrial planets most accessible to detailed characterisation. We report a sub-Earth-sized transiting planet candidate in the wide (17.6") M-dwarf binary GJ 774 at 12.86 pc, most likely orbiting the M2.5 primary GJ 774 A (TIC 351339274). The signal was a SPOC multi-sector threshold-crossing event (MES = 7.95) and is not a TESS Object of Interest. In eight TESS sectors (2019-2026) a 1.28-h transit recurs every 4.225138 +/- 0.000010 d with a box-mean depth of 365 +/- 32 ppm in A's light. The 2026 data, which entered neither the SPOC search nor our selection, show it at the ephemeris predicted from 2019-2023 data (304 +/- 43 ppm; none of 10^5 phase-scrambled versions of the 2026 data is as deep). The per-target false-alarm probability is < 0.03 at 95%. Odd/even, secondary-eclipse, archival-plate and Gaia radial-velocity tests exclude unrelated blended eclipsing binaries and eclipsing companions on 4.2-d orbits, and hierarchical eclipsing binaries are improbable. The stars are 0.85 TESS pixel apart, so the TRICERATOPS false-positive probability (0.26) is set by a planet on GJ 774 B. B is disfavoured because its own light does not dim enough: PRF-deblended photometry gives 109 +/- 115 ppm in B's light, against 1089 ppm required if B were the host. Conditional on a point source at A or at B, the joint host model gives P(A)=0.59-0.97 (0.97 for the native target-pixel baseline). Over all sectors the PRF photometry is consistent with A, but in the out-of-sample 2026 data 40% of the deficit appears at B's position, an unexplained 2-3 sigma (PSF-model and depth dependent) tension with host A. On A the planet has R_p=0.70 +/- 0.06 R_Earth, S=15.0 +/- 1.8 S_Earth and T_eq=548 +/- 16 K. It is not validated; resolved ground-based photometry of the pair would test host B directly.
item.dc:creator: Jaden Tripp

item.title: The science case for an in-situ measurement platform in the Venus clouds
item.description: arXiv:2610.27038v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The next step for Venus exploration after the remote sensing missions of the early 2030s will be in-situ aerial platforms, the Venus equivalent of rovers for Mars. Sophisticated Venus balloon technology is already under development and presents an opportunity for the United Kingdom to act as a bilateral partner in missions exploring key questions about the volcanic and geological history of Venus, the potential habitability of the Venus clouds, and Venus as an analogue for exoplanets. White paper written for the UKSA Space Frontiers 2035 programme.
item.dc:creator: Maureen Cohen, Joanna Egan, Martin Airey, Karen Aplin, Gilles Bailet, Paul Byrne, Chris Castelli, Charles Cockell, Nathan Mayne, Blair McGinness, Ingo Mueller-Wodarg, John Plane, Julia Semprich, Denis Sergeev, Wencheng Shao, Alexander Stott, Roland Young

item.title: Phakoseismology: Asteroseismology of gravitationally microlensed stars
item.description: arXiv:2610.28005v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Asteroseismology relies on disk-integrated photometry or radial velocities, in which geometric cancellation suppresses modes of high spherical degree ($l\geq4$). Observations are thus limited to deeply penetrating, low-degree modes, leaving the outer envelope inaccessible. We investigate whether a high-magnification microlensing event can temporarily lift this limitation by differentially magnifying the surface of an oscillating source star. We modelled the visibility of solar-like oscillations during microlensing, weighting the surface by limb darkening and the local magnification. We computed multiplet visibilities and the power distribution among azimuthal components, and built a likelihood model for recovering the 3D spin-axis orientation from resolved rotational multiplets. When the lens-source separation becomes comparable to the source's angular radius, the magnification gradient acts as a transient spatial filter that breaks the symmetry of disk integration, raising high-degree mode visibilities by up to three orders of magnitude. The same non-axisymmetric weighting makes the relative power of azimuthal components depend on both the inclination and sky-projected azimuth of the spin axis, imprinting the full spin orientation onto the power spectrum. With $5\%$ relative-power uncertainties, we recover the orientation to $\sigma_i=2.9^\circ$ and $\sigma_\gamma=11.5^\circ$. Microlensing thus does more than amplify distant stars: its magnification pattern enables spatially selective asteroseismology. The effect is strongest for rare close encounters and unlikely to support large samples, and the newly visible high-degree modes will overlap with rotationally split and mixed modes, complicating mode identification. Nevertheless, individual high-quality events may open a window on envelope physics and spin geometries for stars in the Galactic bulge and beyond.
item.dc:creator: Marcus L. Marcussen, Mikkel N. Lund

item.title: Coevolution of Dust Growth and Gravitational Instability in Massive Protostellar Disks
item.description: arXiv:2610.28331v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Massive protostellar disks are expected to sustain high accretion rates through gravitational instability, while dust growth may modify their opacity, cooling efficiency, and stability. Conversely, the time-dependent and nonaxisymmetric structures produced by gravitational instability may regulate the local conditions for dust growth. However, the coupled evolution of dust growth and gravitational instability in massive protostellar disks has not yet been explored self-consistently. We present two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations that follow gas dynamics, dust growth, and opacity-dependent radiative cooling in a massive protostellar disk. We find that dust grains rapidly grow to millimeter-centimeter sizes shortly after disk formation, substantially reducing the infrared opacity. The enhanced cooling promotes disk fragmentation and produces more frequent accretion-driven luminosity outbursts than in a model without dust growth, with durations and peak luminosities comparable to those observed in massive protostars. Dust growth is broadly regulated by the fragmentation-limited size in dense disk regions, whereas newly formed outer disk regions and low-density regions deviate from this limit because of finite collision timescales and dust transport. These results suggest that dust growth may facilitate episodic accretion and fragmentation, while gravitationally unstable disk structures in turn regulate the dust growth process.
item.dc:creator: Ryota Yamamuro, Ryoki Matsukoba, Kei E. I. Tanaka, Eduard I. Vorobyov

item.title: Data-Driven Ages from Asteroseismology for FGK Dwarfs
item.description: arXiv:2610.28345v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Age is the one of the most difficult stellar properties to constrain. However, upcoming surveys such as PLATO are about to revolutionize our ability to measure FGK dwarf ages with asteroseismology. Here, we use The Cannon to construct a data-driven model for inferring asteroseismic-quality age measurements from large spectroscopic survey observations and demonstrate that forthcoming asteroseismology datasets from future surveys can be leveraged, together with our model, to obtain stellar age samples larger than can be obtained by those surveys alone. We train The Cannon on 323 FGK dwarf stars with asteroseismic age labels from NASA Kepler photometry and high-resolution spectra from the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE). We apply our model to FGK dwarfs from the Kepler survey that exhibit solar-like oscillations and reproduce their reported asteroseismic-quality ages with an RMS scatter of 1.0 Gyr. We then apply our model to the sample of 3810 Kepler FGK dwarfs with APOGEE spectra to infer data-driven asteroseismic ages. We repeat this for the larger sample of 48,828 FGK dwarfs with APOGEE spectra. Our work demonstrates that data-driven methods can robustly reproduce asteroseismic ages for FGK dwarfs. These methods will be invaluable tools for extending asteroseimology measurements from upcoming surveys (e.g., PLATO) to much larger stellar samples.
item.dc:creator: Christopher Lam, Aida Behmard, Sarah Ballard, Andrew R. Casey, Jamie N. Tayar, Jared A. Goldberg

item.title: A Solar Optical Clock
item.description: arXiv:2610.28485v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Precision spectroscopy underpins quantum sensing, atomic timekeeping, and the search for terrestrial-mass exoplanets. Finding an Earth-Sun analog requires fractional splitting of spectral features that rivals the precision of the best laboratory spectroscopy. This corresponds to resolution of a few parts in $10^5$ of a typical stellar spectral line, or a Doppler velocity precision of less than 10 cm s$^{-1}$. Only a few astrophysical spectrometers reach this regime, and only by dispersing starlight with large gratings and averaging thousands of lines. Here, we show that comparable precision can be achieved on a single solar line by leveraging techniques used in quantum sensors and optical clocks. A laser is frequency-locked to the 1565 nm solar Fe I line by coupling to a single mode of the solar thermal field and counted against an optical frequency comb referenced to the SI second, thus creating a solar optical clock. Operating at the fundamental photon-noise limit of thermal heterodyne spectroscopy, we achieve centroid precision of one part in $10^9$ of the optical frequency, or 30 cm s$^{-1}$ in radial velocity. We recover the Sun's five-minute acoustic oscillations and the expected Rossiter-McLaughlin signal during a solar eclipse. Combining these techniques from quantum sensing with a thirty-meter-class telescope could enable our demonstrated precision on the nearest Sun-like stars in a few hours. Multiplexing such absolute frequency measurements across lines with different magnetic sensitivity and formation depth would reduce averaging time and help disentangle stellar granulation and activity from the Doppler signature of terrestrial exoplanets, providing new approaches to address some of the most demanding measurements in astrophysical spectroscopy.
item.dc:creator: Connor Fredrick, Ryan K. Cole, Ryan Terrien, Suvrath Mahadevan, Scott A. Diddams

item.title: Automated optimization of solar energetic particle acceleration and transport parameters against five-spacecraft observations of the 9 October 2021 event
item.description: arXiv:2610.28603v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Solar energetic particle (SEP) events threaten space infrastructure, yet physics-based prediction models depend on numerous poorly constrained free parameters. We introduce the Fujitsu Solar Energetic particle Intelligent Tuning and Evaluation Network (SEITEN), which couples the SUSANOO MHD model of CME propagation to SEPIF, a diffusive shock acceleration and focused transport model, through the shock conditions SUSANOO supplies, and automatically optimizes the free parameters of the particle model against the SEP event of 9 October 2021. The mean free path and the injection efficiency vary independently along each magnetic field line and heliolongitudinal bin, giving a 19-dimensional problem solved by quasi-Monte Carlo sampling followed by a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. The optimized model reproduces proton flux profiles at five spacecraft with a mean absolute error of $\approx 0.45$ in $\log_{10}$ flux, and the inferred mean free paths show a clear east-west structure; these are effective parameters conditional on the assumed transport geometry. Six independent runs show that whether mean free paths or injection efficiencies dominate depends on the MHD shock strength, and that injection efficiencies differ by orders of magnitude between MHD configurations despite nearly identical fit quality. Joint MHD-SEP parameter estimation is therefore a necessary next step towards generalized, operational SEP forecasting.
item.dc:creator: Hiroyuki Tako Ishikawa, Naho Fujita, Yuta Kato, Miki Kurihara, Takashi Minoshima, Daikou Shiota, Kazumasa Iwai, Marco Pinto, Ant\'onio Pessanha Gomes, Go Murakami, Kanya Kusano, Chihiro Mitsuda

item.title: The Effect of Adiabatic Index on Radius Evolution and the Mass Loss
item.description: arXiv:2606.17143v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Models that track the size evolution of exoplanets often assume a prescribed initial thermal state or a single adiabatic index to describe the planetary interior structure, the latter of which is taken to be $\gamma \sim1.4$ which is likely appropriate for evolved planets ($\gtrsim$1 Gyr). Extrapolating this high $\gamma$ to earlier ages (down to $\sim$million years old) is problematic since, according to thermodynamics, the adiabatic index of young planets is $\sim$1.2, which is low enough to drastically change how interior mass is distributed. We quantify the effect of varying the adiabatic index from 1.2 to 1.4 on the expected radius of the exoplanet over time. We find that envelopes of larger adiabatic indices start puffier with all else equal and undergo faster radius contraction with accelerated mass loss. Assumption of high $\gamma$ can therefore overestimate the effect of mass loss in shaping the exoplanetary population, especially when young planets are considered. We highlight the need for a more careful consideration of the initial thermal condition of planets in evolutionary models to properly interpret the radii measurements of exoplanets.

item.title: Thermal Evolution of Lava Planets Across System Ages: Predictions for Hell of a Survey
item.description: arXiv:2609.20155v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ultra-short-period (USP) rocky exoplanets can have dayside temperatures high enough to maintain permanent magma oceans, sitting at the intersection of interior geophysics and atmospheric chemistry. Coupled feedbacks between the molten surface and outgassed atmosphere can sustain or enhance a volatile envelope, while stellar interactions can erode it. Understanding which outcome prevails, and its observable imprint, requires a multi-target approach across planets at different stages of thermal evolution. We present predictions for the five targets of JWST Cycle 4 program 8864: TOI-1807 b, TOI-2260 b, TOI-431 b, TOI-6255 b, and TOI-2431 b. Using the PROTEUS coupled interior-atmosphere framework, we construct a simulation grid and classify outcomes into six categories, defined by the final interior melt state and by whether the planet retains a detectable atmosphere thick enough to redistribute heat to the nightside. For targets retaining a non-negligible volatile envelope, our models predict higher partial pressures for most species when the surface is molten, except for S$_{2}$, whose enhancement in the solid regime suggests it may serve as a tracer of interior melt state. Despite some targets showing outcomes across multiple scenarios, most tend toward a bare-rock end-member, with global melt fraction $\leq$ 20\% and atmospheric retention sensitive to escape efficiency. Our analysis reveals a minimum escape efficiency threshold below which volatile envelopes survive under energy-limited escape, constraining the conditions required for atmosphere survival on irradiated rocky planets. These predictions will guide interpretation of MIRI-LRS phase curve observations and identify which targets and features best discriminate between competing geophysical states.

item.title: A faint dust ring beyond the compact disk of Sz 76
item.description: arXiv:2610.09881v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We report new ALMA Band 7 high-resolution ($\sim$0.05$^{''}$) continuum and $^{12}\text{CO}\ (J=3\text{--}2)$ observations of the disk around the young low-mass star Sz 76. Visibility-plane modeling reveals a previously undetected, faint outer dust ring centered at $\sim$45 au surrounding the compact central disk. Including this low-surface-brightness feature increases the characteristic dust radius from $R_{\text{dust,68}} \approx 7$ au to $41$ au. Combined with an outer gas extent of $R_{\text{CO,68}} \approx 77$ au, the resulting gas-to-dust size ratio decreases from an extreme value of $\sim$11 to $\sim$2, placing Sz 76 in line with typical protoplanetary disks and contradicting a scenario of unimpeded inward radial drift. These results demonstrate that spatial filtering or limited surface-brightness sensitivity can severely underestimate disk sizes, highlighting the necessity of multi-scale observations to properly identify dust traps and accurately constrain disk evolution.

item.title: Kratos-polrad: Novel GPU system for Monte-Carlo simulations with consistent polarization calculations
item.description: arXiv:2512.01283v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Polarized radiation serves as a vital diagnostic tool in astrophysics, providing unique insights into magnetic field geometries, scattering processes, and three-dimensional structures in diverse astrophysical scenarios. To address these applications, we present Kratos_polrad, a novel GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo Radiative Transfer code built upon the heterogeneous computing framework of Kratos, designed for self-consistent and efficient polarization calculations. It utilizes a comprehensive treatment of the Stokes parameters throughout photon propagation, featuring grain-lab frame transformations using quaternion algebra and a consistent analytical integration of polarized extinction and emission within each cell, which are useful in modeling radiative transfer processes with scatterings by aligned dust grains. The code implements two-step polarimetry imaging that decouples Monte Carlo sampling of scattering physics from imaging geometry, enabling efficient synthesis maximizing the utilization of photon packets. Extensive validation against analytical solutions and established codes demonstrates accurate treatment of diverse polarization phenomena, including self-scattering polarization, dichroic extinction in aligned dust grains, and complex polarization patterns in twisted magnetic field configurations. By leveraging massive GPU parallelism, optimized memory access patterns, and analytical approaches for optically thick cells, Kratos_polrad achieves performance improvements of ~10^2 times compared to CPU-based methods, enabling previously prohibitive studies in polarimetric astrophysics.
item.dc:creator: Haifeng Yang, Lile Wang

item.title: Resonant lunar tides of Earth's core and basal magma ocean
item.description: arXiv:2606.16340v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Earth's magnetic field is generated by fluid motion in the liquid-metal core and has been active for billions of years. However, prior to the onset of inner-core growth, the sources of mechanical power that drove the geodynamo remain uncertain. During this period, the core may have been overlain by a basal magma ocean (BMO), creating two immiscible fluid layers separated by a density interface, beneath the solid mantle. We develop a theory for lunar tides in this core--BMO system, in which the tidal potential acts on the density contrast between the two layers. The resulting dynamics differ fundamentally from previous models driven by imposed deformation of the core's bounding envelope. In the inviscid limit, the response transitions from an equilibrium tide to an interfacial gravity wave as forcing frequency increases. The two regimes are separated by a resonance that occurs when the forcing frequency matches the natural frequency of the degree-2, order-2 interfacial mode. The inviscid core flow is formally identical to the canonical elliptical vortex, linking the problem to the theory of elliptical instability. Finite viscosity regularises the resonance, introduces phase lag and generates oscillatory boundary layers. Combined with parameterised models of lunar recession and BMO crystallisation, the theory predicts enhanced core-boundary ellipticity, core-flow speed, magnetic Reynolds number and instability metrics, particularly near resonance. These results identify a previously unexplored mechanism for tidally driven flow in differentiated planetary bodies and show that a BMO can enhance tidal coupling to the core, potentially contributing to dynamo action.
